headline: 75.9 on the Bight buoy: bluefin working the Mud Hole lumps, mahi stacked on the pot lines
subhead: Warm water pushing into the inshore lumps has bluefin and mahi cooperating, but the sea bass numbers are the sure thing this week.
body_markdown:
75.9. That's the reading off the Bight buoy this week, and it's the number that's had my phone going since Tuesday morning. Doesn't sound like much until you remember what that water was doing three weeks ago — mid-60s, gray, dead current. Now we've got a warm tongue pushing up against the edge of the Mud Hole and it's dragging bait and bluefin with it. Seas are running 3.6 feet at 6 seconds out of the south, which isn't glass but it's workable — anything 26 feet and up should have no trouble getting out and getting home dry.

The Mud Hole lumps have been the play. I'm marking bait stacked hard on the northeast lump in 110 to 130 feet, and we've had bluefin from schoolie size up to mid-40s class fish coming through on small blue-and-white spreader bars and cedar plugs run tight to the boat — 60 to 90 feet back, no farther. When the fish get finicky, which they have on the slower tide stages, we've switched to butterfish chunks drifted off the transom over the lump edge and that's when the better-grade fish show. It's not a wide-open bite — two out of my last three trips out there connected solid, one was a grind for three fish in six hours — but for early August that's a number I'll take. If the warm filament holds where it's sitting, I'd expect the Mud Hole to keep producing through the weekend. If it slides off to the east like these things do in a hurry, Klondike is the backup — same depth range, same lump structure, and we've had a few yellowfin mixed in out there on the edge where that warmer water is bleeding westward off the canyon breaks. Small purple-and-black Ilanders on the short rigger, green machines out back — nothing fancy, just get the spread in front of them.

We flagged this pattern last week — said the tuna bite would hold steady as long as this calm stretch stuck around, and that's exactly what's played out. The high pressure hasn't budged, the current's cooperating, and the fish are where the temperature says they should be. That won't last forever in August — watch the tropics — but for now it's the setup you want.

Mahi are the other story worth telling. We've been finding them stacked under the pot buoys working the stretch between Barnegat Ridge and the inshore edge, and under any weed line holding bait — you don't need much, a mat the size of a car hood will hold a pack. Small bailer-class fish mostly, two to five pounds, with the occasional three- or four-pounder that'll make you think you found a bigger school than you did. Sabiki-teased ballyhoo strips on light spinning gear has been the most fun way to work them, though a chunk line off butterfish will pull them up from under the structure if they're sulking deep. Best window has been late morning once the sun's had a chance to warm the surface layer — that's when they come up and show themselves.

Bottom fishing is still the most dependable thing going on this beat, and it's not close. Sea bass are holding heavy on the reef and wreck network — Axel Carlson Reef in 60 to 70 feet has been giving up good numbers of keepers, and there's a wreck sitting in 75 feet off the Ridge that's been holding some genuine jumbos, four-pound class fish, on bucktail-and-Gulp combos bounced right on the structure. Shrewsbury Rocks has been more of a numbers spot than a size spot lately — lots of 12- to 13-inch fish mixed with enough keepers to make it worth the anchor drop. Triple Wrecks, when we've had the current cooperating, has produced the best average size of anywhere I fished this month. Squid strips or clam on a double bottom rig, straight up and down, patience over structure — that's still the whole game. No surprises there, and that consistency is exactly why I keep coming back to those numbers year after year.

Blackfish season's closed through the summer so that box stays shut for now, and cod isn't a realistic target with water this warm — that's a late-fall conversation.

Looking ahead, if this high-pressure stretch holds through the weekend the way it's been sitting, I'd keep working the Mud Hole lumps early and be ready to run to Klondike if the temp break shifts. Watch the wave state — if that southerly swell builds past four feet, the smaller boats should sit tight and let the bigger fleet work it. The sea bass grounds don't care what the weather's doing offshore, so that's your fallback on any day the ocean looks unfriendly past the three-mile line. I'll be out on the lumps again this week chasing that warm water while it's still sitting where we want it — worth the run if you can get out before it moves.
